A typeface for base64

Sixty four symbols
you can say out loud.

Base64 is text no one can read. aGVsbG8gd29ybGQ cannot be compared at a glance, dictated over a phone, or checked by eye. Sixty Four gives each of the 64 characters a symbol instead — and encodes it twice, once as colour and once as hatch, so it survives a black-and-white printer and colour blindness alike.

The alphabet

Four tiers, sixteen shapes.

Every value decomposes cleanly: value = tier × 16 + class × 4 + shape. Read the column for the shape, the row for the tier, and you have the number.

Light and dark

Legible on either ground.

The empty and solid tiers paint with the text colour rather than a stored one, so they invert with the page instead of vanishing into it — which is why a solid symbol reads black on white and white on black. The dotted and striped tiers switch to a lighter blue and red on dark grounds. Both renderings are shown here at once, whichever theme you happen to be reading in.

Which is also why those two tiers are called Blank and Fill rather than white and black. They hold no colour to be named after — only Blue and Red do — and a tier named “black” would be telling you the opposite of what you were looking at on half the pages it is read on.

Reading one symbol

Shape, then texture.

The symbol p
Shape Fire

Elements, shape 1 of 0–3. Carries the low two bits.

Texture Dots · Blue

Tier 2 of 0–3. Tier and hatch say the same thing, so either one on its own is enough to read it.

Therefore p = 41

2 × 16 + 2 × 4 + 1 = 41

Saying them out loud

Shape, then texture.

Name the shape, then the texture. Four texture words cover every tier — blank, lines, dots, fill — so any of the sixty-four is two plain words, and a string can be read down a phone line without anyone spelling anything.

AblankNo fill
wlinesLine
gdotsDots
QfillTotal fill

One from each class, one of each texture:

Across blankA · 0
Vdiamonds fillV · 21
qair dotsq · 42
9flower lines9 · 61

Without colour

The hatch carries it alone.

This section is set in Sixty Four Mono, which has no colour tables at all — nothing to strip, nothing to fall back from. The texture is doing all the work, and all sixty-four stay distinct. This is what a photocopy, a laser printer, or an e-ink screen gives you.

AblankNo fill
wlinesLine
gdotsDots
QfillTotal fill

All sixty-four, in value order:

ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789+/

Ships as SixtyFourMono-Regular.ttf and sixty-four-mono.css. The colour font keeps these same outlines as its fallback, so a renderer that cannot do COLR lands here rather than on nothing.

If the font never loads

It degrades to itself.

Nothing here is an image, an icon set, or a substitution. The characters underneath are ordinary base64 — the font only changes how they are drawn. Take it away and you are left with exactly the string you started with, which is not true of any approach that swaps the text for pictures.

Select and copy

Drag across the symbols and you have selected base64. What lands on the clipboard is the string, not a row of pictures.

Find in page

Ctrl+F searches the real characters. So does your editor, your terminal, and grep.

Screen readers

Announce the base64 itself. There are no alt texts to write and none to get wrong.

Everything else

Diffs, logs, curl, a text field, a tool that has never heard of this font. The bytes never changed.

Using it

One file, no hosting.

sixty-four.css carries the font inside it as a data URI, so there is no second request and nothing to upload. Link it and add the class.

<link rel="stylesheet" href="sixty-four.css">

<span class="sixty-four">U2l4dHkgRm91ciBtYWtlcyBi</span>

Outside the browser, install SixtyFour-Regular.ttf and set it as the font in any editor or terminal — every glyph is one em wide, so columns stay aligned. Where colour fonts are not supported the same file falls back to the hatched outlines rather than to nothing. Sixty Four Mono ships separately for anywhere that prefers no colour table at all.

URL-safe base64 works too: -, _ map onto the same symbols as + and /, so JWTs and file-safe encodings need no conversion.
